title: Секрет настоящего Шефа  (The Secret of a True Chef)

segments.t: Visiting the hospital with fresh food, Lyova confesses to Viktor Petrovich that the diplomatic trick backfired and the kitchen is still in chaos. Barinov explains that the only way to keep line cooks in check is to be a ruthless bastard, something gentle Lyova struggles to do.
А то у меня вся постель в крошках.
Вообще-то у меня только один способ действовал.
Понимаешь, Лёва, чтобы быть настоящим шефом.
Now let's go back through the conversation line by line.
'Hello, Petrovich.' Max naturally directs this formal greeting in front of Barinov using "zdravstvuyte" ("hello") — the polite Russian greeting that literally wishes the other person good health.
'Yes. Hello.' Barinov smoothly gives this formal greeting at this moment using "zdravstvuyte" ("hello") — the polite Russian greeting that literally wishes the other person good health.
'How is your health?' Lyova quizzes briskly where this conversation is heading next.

'Thank you very much.' Max directly drops this word of thanks at this moment using "spasibo" ("thank you") — the everyday word for "thank you", which grew out of the old blessing "spasi Bog" ("God save you").
А то у меня вся постель в крошках.
'Otherwise my whole bed is full of crumbs.' Pushing back plainly before Max, Barinov links the Russian words directly in the present with no word for "am", "is", or "are" needed.
'How are things going in the kitchen?' Lyova asks wryly before Max can change the subject.
'Are you completely joking or what?' Max fires back firmly around Barinov and lands on "shutish" ("are joking", built on "shutit") to keep the statement grounded.
Вообще-то у меня только один способ действовал.
'Actually, only one method ever worked for me.' Jumping in quietly before Max, Barinov drops in "voobshche" ("in general, altogether") to sum up the whole situation at once.
Понимаешь, Лёва, чтобы быть настоящим шефом.
'You see, Lyova, in order to be a real head chef.' Max follows up candidly facing Barinov, grounding the moment in plain reality.
'Which method? You see?' Max reacts pointedly right here and centers the thought on "ponimayesh" ("do you understand", from "ponimat") without wasting a word.
'You have to be a real bastard.' Checking on the creep on the spot, Barinov leans on "nado" ("it is necessary, one needs to"), which carries the whole predicate in Russian without needing "it is".
'And being a bastard, Lyova, is not easy.' Max answers plainly toward Lyova, so Lyova knows he is not just making small talk.

'All right, go back to work.' Max firmly sends this word of agreement without hesitation using "ladno" ("alright") — built from the old Russian root for harmony and order, used every day for "okay, fine".
А то у меня вся постель в крошках.
Вообще-то у меня только один способ действовал.
Понимаешь, Лёва, чтобы быть настоящим шефом.

That wraps up this scene as lyova visits Chef Barinov in the hospital to admit that the reconciliation trick failed, and Barinov explains that to command the kitchen, a chef must act like a ruthless tyrant. Until next time!
